content: Below is a detailed explanation of the key aspects of care: General Management Plan Children with complicated SAM are managed in two phases: stabilization (days 1–7) and rehabilitation (weeks 2–6). The stabilization phase focuses on addressing life-threatening conditions, while the rehabilitation phase promotes recovery and weight gain. Key Conditions to Address in Stabilization Phase: 1. Hypoglycemia: All children with SAM are at risk of low blood sugar. On admission, they should immediately receive a feed or 10% glucose/sucrose solution (50 mL orally or via nasogastric tube). Blood glucose should be monitored, and frequent 2-hourly feeds are essential. If the child is unconscious, administer IV 10% glucose at 5 mL/kg or nasogastric glucose if IV access is unavailable. 2. Hypothermia: Hypothermia is common in malnourished children and often indicates infection or hypoglycemia. If the axillary temperature is below 35°C (95°F), assume hypothermia. Rewarm the child using warm clothing, blankets, or skin-to-skin contact (Kangaroo technique). Avoid drafts and monitor temperature regularly. 3. Dehydration: Clinical signs of dehydration may be unreliable in SAM. Oral or nasogastric rehydration with ReSoMal (rehydration solution for malnutrition) is preferred over IV fluids unless the child is in shock. Rehydrate slowly (5–10 mL/kg per hour for up to 12 hours). 4. Electrolyte Imbalance: All children with SAM have potassium and magnesium deficiencies. These should be corrected over two weeks by adding potassium (3–4 mmol/kg/day) and magnesium (0.4–0.6 mmol/kg/day) to feeds. Avoid high sodium intake, as it can worsen edema. 5. Infections: Signs of infection may be absent in SAM, so assume all children have an infection and start broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately. For uncomplicated cases, oral amoxicillin is given for 5 days. For complicated cases, parenteral antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin and gentamicin) are used. 6. Micronutrient Deficiencies: Provide multivitamins, including vitamin A, folic acid, zinc, and copper. Do not give iron initially, as it can exacerbate infections. Iron supplementation begins in the rehabilitation phase once the child has a good appetite and is gaining weight. 7. Feeding: Initiate feeding with F-75 therapeutic milk, which is low in protein and sodium but high in energy. Feed every 2 hours for the first 24 hours, then every 2–3 hours. Gradually transition to F-100 or ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) during the rehabilitation phase. Monitoring During Stabilization: Blood glucose should be checked every 30 minutes if initially low. Monitor for signs of overhydration during rehydration (e.g., increased respiratory rate, pulse rate, or liver size). Rehabilitation Phase The focus shifts to catch-up growth and recovery: 1. Feeding: Transition from F-75 to F-100 or RUTF over 2–3 days. Gradually increase feed volumes to achieve 150–220 kcal/kg/day and 4–6 g protein/kg/day. Encourage frequent, unlimited feeding. 2. Weight Monitoring: Weigh the child daily and calculate weight gain every 3 days. Good weight gain is defined as >10 g/kg/day. Poor weight gain (<5 g/kg/day) requires reassessment for infections or inadequate intake. 3. Sensory Stimulation: Provide toys and play activities to promote mental and emotional recovery. Encourage caregiver involvement in comforting, feeding, and playing with the child. Special Considerations 1. Severe Anemia: Blood transfusion is indicated if hemoglobin (Hb) is <4 g/dL or 4–6 g/dL with respiratory distress. Transfuse slowly (10 mL/kg over 3 hours) and administer furosemide to prevent fluid overload. 2. Eye Problems: If there are signs of vitamin A deficiency (e.g., corneal clouding), administer vitamin A on days 1, 2, and 14. Provide additional care for corneal ulcers, such as antibiotic eye drops and saline-soaked eye pads. 3. HIV Testing: In areas with high HIV prevalence, test children with SAM for HIV. Start antiretroviral therapy (ART) after stabilizing metabolic complications and infections. Discharge Criteria A child can be discharged from nutritional care when: They are breastfeeding effectively or feeding well with replacement feeds. They have adequate weight gain (e.g., weight-for-length ≥ -2 z-scores). They are linked to community follow-up and support. Infants Under 6 Months Severe acute malnutrition in infants under 6 months is less common but requires special attention. Admission is necessary if there are complicating factors such as ineffective breastfeeding, recent weight loss, or bilateral edema. Treatment includes re-establishing exclusive breastfeeding or providing infant formula/F-75 as a supplement. Monitor closely for salt and urea excretion issues, especially in hot climates.
